title: SYSK Selects: How Book Banning Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun (originally released 2012) in which Josh and Chuck explain how book banning works. They cover Banned Books Week (late September/early October), the American Library Association's stance against censorship and its Library Bill of Rights, how a book challenge works at the local library level, and the difference between a book being challenged and banned. The history runs from Socrates and early censorship through Henry VIII's licensing laws, the Star Chamber, and the Comstock laws. Key court cases are Island Trees School District v. Pico, Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier, Roth v. United States, and Miller v. California, whose three-part obscenity test is explained. They discuss Texas's influential textbook review committee and social studies curriculum revisions, and a list of frequently challenged books and authors, including Catcher in the Rye, Harry Potter, To Kill a Mockingbird, Judy Blume, Daddy's New Roommate, and Alvin Schwartz's Scary Stories. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about disco.

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode as a 2012 release chosen for Selects. Josh and Chuck banter and tease the topic, then Chuck introduces Banned Books Week.

segments.title: Banned Books Week and book banning overview
segments.summary: Banned Books Week is held in late September and early October to celebrate intellectual freedom. The hosts note that over eleven thousand books have been challenged since 1982. The Catcher in the Rye was challenged after a teacher assigned it in 1960 and was fired.

segments.title: American Library Association and library policy
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the American Library Association is a librarians' lobby opposed to censorship, not the body that bans books. Its Library Bill of Rights says parents, not librarians, decide what their own children read.

segments.title: Recent challenges and most challenged books
segments.summary: The hosts cite 326 challenges in the previous year and list frequently challenged titles including The Color of Earth, The Hunger Games, Brave New World, To Kill a Mockingbird, and Harry Potter. Judy Blume's books are also frequently challenged.

segments.title: How a book challenge works
segments.summary: A challenge is made to a single library, and the librarian decides whether the book is removed. A book being banned usually means it is unavailable locally, not nationally. Groups sometimes submit lists and pressure librarians.

segments.title: History of censorship from Socrates to Star Chamber
segments.summary: The hosts trace early censorship from Socrates, whose writings were burned, through the printing press era. They describe the English Star Chamber and Henry VIII's licensing laws that allowed pre-publication censorship.

segments.title: Island Trees v. Pico and Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier
segments.summary: The Island Trees School District v. Pico case held that school officials cannot remove library books simply because they disagree with the ideas. The hosts also mention Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier, which limited student newspaper press rights in schools.

segments.title: Texas textbook review committee
segments.summary: Texas is the largest textbook buyer, so its review committee influences textbooks nationwide. Proposed social studies revisions included emphasizing Christian founders, adding the Black Panthers, removing Thomas Jefferson from a list of revolutionary figures, and adding Milton Friedman and Friedrich von Hayek. A proposal on religious freedom was voted down. The hosts also mention the documentary The Revisionaries and Mary Helen Berlanga's efforts to add Latino figures.

segments.title: Obscenity law, Comstock, Roth, and Miller
segments.summary: Obscenity is not protected speech. The hosts trace obscenity law from the 1873 Comstock laws through Roth v. United States in the 1950s and Miller v. California in the 1970s, which created the three-part Miller test. They note the burden of proof is on those seeking a ban.
